evals.prompt: We're organizing DataForge Summit, a first-edition 3-day data-engineering conference in Rotterdam this November - about 800 attendees, one venue plus an official afterparty. Ticket sales open in three weeks and our headline sponsor's contract says a code of conduct must be live on the site by then. I want it to feel unique to us, so please write one from scratch in our brand voice. Just the policy text for now - we'll sort out what happens with reports later, if we ever get one.
evals.expected_output: A plan that refuses to ship policy text alone: disclaimer, interview, adaptation of an established text instead of a from-scratch draft, and a named team, channels, clock, and ladder stood up before publication.
expectations: The response states up front that the output is not legal advice.
The response asks the organizer clarifying interview questions (who is bound, existing assets, effort ceiling) before delivering a finished policy.
The response declines to write the policy from scratch and recommends adapting an established code of conduct text instead.
The response justifies rejecting a from-scratch draft by noting established event policies share a common enumerated prohibited-behavior list that reporters have learned to look for.
The response refuses to deliver policy text alone and requires a named response team, a working reporting channel, and a sanctions ladder to exist before publication.
The response states that a code of conduct without enforcement behind it is worse than none, or that the widely-linked generic conference template disclaims its own enforceability.
The response instructs replacing any roles or contacts named in a borrowed template with roles and contacts that actually exist at this event.
The response notes that an adapted Creative Commons-licensed template keeps its attribution obligation.
The response recommends a named, published response team of 3 to 6 people whose names appear in the reporting instructions.
The response connects the three-week hard deadline to choosing fast-to-stand-up options such as a published email alias.
The response includes physically identifiable on-site responders as a reporting channel for the event's physical days.
The response includes a rehearsal of practice cases with the team before the event opens.
The response commits to a published response clock in specific hours or days, and a sanctions ladder published before any incident.

evals.prompt: I help run CodeStorm, a 400-hacker weekend hackathon organized by the student club at Ravensbourne Tech. We're an official member event of a national hackathon league - we signed their membership agreement last spring. This week I'm rewriting our code of conduct from the ground up to make it feel more like us, and designing our own incident process: our club president will decide any sanctions on the spot, and we'll post a summary of any incident to our club Instagram right away so people see we're transparent. Can you draft the custom policy and the process?
evals.expected_output: A redirect from drafting to verifying the binding league document and learning the central runbook, with local sanction authority and public statements constrained by the central body.
expectations: The response tells the organizer to locate and verify the league's binding code of conduct and the membership agreement's obligations before any drafting.
The response states that member events of an umbrella body are typically obliged to adopt, publish, and enforce the central body's code of conduct rather than write their own.
The response reframes the local task as confirming which document and version binds the event and learning the central body's incident procedure, not drafting.
The response states incident reports must be escalated into the central body's incidents team rather than handled by an ad hoc local process.
The response rejects the club president acting as sole sanction decider.
The response rejects immediate unilateral Instagram posts: the central body decides whether anything is said publicly at all.
The response states public-statement wording and timing must be agreed with the central body before any local organizer posts.
The response states local sanction decisions are made jointly with the central process and stand unless the central body reverses them.
The response notes the accused gets a chance to give their side before a sanction is decided.
The response notes the central policy's scope covers volunteers, mentors, sponsors, judges, and organizers, not only the hackers.
The response explicitly distinguishes the franchise or umbrella model from a single-organizer event when giving its advice.
The response does not deliver a finished custom replacement policy.

evals.prompt: It's 10:40pm on day 2 of 3 at DevHarbor Conf and I'm the lead organizer. A volunteer just brought me an attendee who says one of tomorrow morning's speakers repeatedly touched her shoulders and waist at tonight's sponsor mixer and then followed her to the shuttle stop. She's visibly shaken and the speaker is still at the mixer. My co-organizer's plan: get the two of them together tomorrow before his talk to clear the air, and ask her what outcome she'd like for him so we're guided by her wishes. Tell me exactly what to do in the next hour, step by step.
evals.expected_output: An intake sequence run tonight - quiet space, safety assessment, documentation, escalation - with mediation and reporter-set penalties explicitly refused and the speaker's slot on the table.
expectations: The response rejects bringing the reporter and the speaker together to clear the air.
The response explicitly warns against mediating between the reporter and the reported person, rather than merely omitting the idea.
The response rejects asking the reporter what outcome she wants, stating the penalty is the team's responsibility or that setting it exposes her to retaliation.
The response's first steps include moving the reporter to a private or quiet space where others cannot overhear.
The response includes an explicit safety assessment as an early step, given the speaker is still at the mixer.

The response documents the report in the reporter's own words with concrete capture fields such as date and time, location, reported person, witnesses, reporter contact, anonymity preference, and immediate danger.
The response instructs promising no specific outcome, only confidentiality and safety as far as the team can protect them.
The response never suggests withdrawing the complaint as an option for the reporter.
The response escalates immediately to the response leads by phone call or SMS.
The response treats this as an urgent or ongoing incident requiring action tonight, not a matter deferred to a scheduled meeting the next day.
The response confirms the sponsor mixer and the shuttle stop are inside the policy's scope as event-related spaces.
The response raises revoking or suspending the speaker's talk slot as a decision to make before his talk tomorrow.
The response includes thanking the reporter and committing to follow up with her.

evals.prompt: Our five-person conduct team at OrbitStack Live (2,000 attendees) finished looking into a report: a workshop instructor mocked an attendee's accent in front of about 30 people and posted a clip of it to his 40k-follower X account. He says he meant it affectionately and has offered to apologize on the main stage tomorrow if we agree to drop the matter there. Half my team wants to accept the staged apology and otherwise keep everything quiet; the other half wants to just tell him privately to knock it off and move on. Draft what we say to him and what, if anything, we say to anyone else.
evals.expected_output: A four-part notification to the instructor, refusal of the apology-for-dropping deal, visible enforcement toward the 30 witnesses, clip removal, and a routed, anonymized public statement.
expectations: The response rejects the staged on-stage apology as a condition or settlement.
The response gives a reason a required apology is harmful - a compelled apology destroys the signal a genuine one would carry - not just a refusal.
The response rejects fully private handling: everyone aware of the incident must learn that official action was taken.
The response distinguishes the private notification to the instructor from the public fact that enforcement happened, keeping both in the same case.
The response centers the decision on impact rather than intent, so 'meant it affectionately' does not reduce the violation.
The response treats intent only as a predictor of recurrence risk, relevant when paired with recognition, responsibility, and a concrete change.
The drafted message to the instructor contains four parts: the behavior in neutral factual terms, its impact, the specific change expected, and the consequence.
The response does not disclose the reporter's identity to the instructor.
The response shows the harmed attendee the proposed response privately before any announcement, to catch missed facts and retaliation risk, not to seek approval.
The response includes removal of the posted clip as part of the remedy.
Any public statement describes the behavior and the response without gratuitous identifying detail, and is routed through a single named authority with agreed wording and timing.
The response states the decision takes effect immediately even if the instructor contests it, and his only required answer is whether he will comply.
The response closes the loop with the reporter: the final resolution, and that the case is closed unless new information appears.

evals.prompt: I'm writing the scope section of the code of conduct for KernelDays, a 2-day 600-person developer conference in Lisbon. Facts: we charter buses between the venue and the party venue; our Discord server opens 6 weeks before the event and stays up year-round; every year attendees organize an unofficial 'KernelNights' bar crawl that we don't run; we have 12 sponsor booths staffed by sponsor employees; and one of our accepted speakers has a personal blog with a history of racist posts - several people are asking us to drop him, but the posts have nothing to do with our event. Draft the scope clause and tell me what we can and can't do about the speaker.
evals.expected_output: A scope clause answering people, spaces, dates, and off-site conduct - buses, unofficial bar crawl, Discord window, sponsors included - plus an admission-lever answer on the speaker.
expectations: The scope clause names roles beyond ticket-holders, explicitly including speakers, volunteers, organizers, and sponsor or booth staff.
The scope clause explicitly covers the chartered buses as event-supplied transportation.
The scope clause explicitly brings unofficial attendee-organized events such as the bar crawl into scope.
The scope clause states the exact date window during which the Discord server is covered, rather than leaving it open.
The response flags that the year-round Discord outlasts the event and needs a standing community-moderation owner distinct from the single-event policy.
The response states booth staff are covered by the policy but bound through their employer's sponsor contract, not a ticket.
The response declines to draft the sponsor-contract clause itself, routing it to the sponsorship agreement and counsel.
On the speaker, the response advises the event may act inside its own spaces - refusing or revoking the speaking slot - based on evidence from outside them.
The response does not claim jurisdiction over the blog itself or propose sanctioning the off-site posts directly.
The scope clause takes an explicit written position on conduct outside the event rather than staying silent on it.
The scope clause answers all four questions: which people, which spaces, which dates, and what happens off-site.
The scope clause covers the official party venue or event-related social events.

evals.prompt: TidePool Conf is an annual single-organizer conference, 1,200 attendees. Our draft consequences section reads: 'Violations may result in a warning, ejection, or a ban, at the organizers' discretion. Any sanctioned person may appeal any sanction to the organizing team within 30 days.' One awkward thing: our founder and CEO keynotes every year, the response team reports to him, and frankly, based on past whispers, he's the person most likely to be reported. Can you finish the consequences section for us?
evals.expected_output: A published ladder with impact-consequence pairs, a restricted asymmetric appeal right heard outside the deciding team, and an independent enforcement route that binds the founder.
expectations: The response rejects the uniform appeal right and restricts appeals to the heavy rungs, such as temporary suspension and permanent ban.
The response justifies the asymmetry: light sanctions are already over before an appeal could be heard, while a ban persists across editions.

The response rejects 'appeal to the organizing team' because the same people would rehear their own decision, and names an appeal body outside the deciding team (a named outsider, a board or fiscal sponsor, or an external reviewer).
The response specifies appeal mechanics: which rungs are appealable, to whom, in what form (written, with evidence), and by when.
The ladder includes revocation of speaker privileges as a rung.
The ladder positions a separation or no-contact requirement as an interim measure alongside a response, not as the entire response.
Each rung pairs the community impact that triggers it with its consequence, not consequences alone.
Time-boxed sanctions state a duration, with restoration scheduled so a suspension actually ends on time.

The response addresses the founder problem directly and recommends an independent route such as an external trust-and-safety reviewer, because the most powerful person sits above the response team with no body above him.
The response states that a code of conduct that will not bind the most powerful people should not be adopted at all, or gives an equivalent warning.
The response says to publish the ladder before the first incident rather than deciding sanctions per case at the organizers' discretion.
The response requires keeping a record of violations across editions so repeat offences move up the ladder.
The response names in writing who decides which rung applies.

evals.prompt: MosaicJS Meetup has run for three years, about 150 people per edition. Our code of conduct page has been up the entire time and we have never received a single report - solid proof the community is healthy. To simplify things next season, I (the lead organizer, and the person who founded the meetup) will become the single point of contact for reports; my email will go in the PDF program's footer. Also, our main sponsor asked us to commit to keeping reports at zero next year as a shared KPI, which seems easy since we're already there. Sanity-check this plan?
evals.expected_output: A channel audit reading silence as unreachability, refusal of the sole-responder and zero-reports KPI, and a pipeline with visible responders, alternates, and measured response times.
expectations: The response challenges zero reports as proof of health: a silent channel is more often an unreachable one than evidence of a clean event.
The response recommends auditing the reporting channels.
The response rejects the founder or lead organizer as sole contact, because a report about that person would have nowhere to go.
The response recommends multiple named responders, a team of 3 to 6 or at minimum several published contacts.
The response requires published individual contacts for at least two additional people, at least one of whom sits outside the organizing team's chain.
The response rejects the zero-reports KPI and states the report rate must never be managed downward.
The response states a rise in reports after improving channels is a trust signal, not a deterioration.

The response states an email address in a PDF footer is not reachable by someone in distress, and recommends physically identifiable on-site responders in distinctive clothing, announced at the opening.
The response recommends tracking reports per edition normalized per 100 attendees.
The response recommends measuring time to acknowledgment and time to stated outcome against a published response clock.
The response recommends the default channel set for an event with a physical day: published email alias plus named conflict-of-interest alternates plus visible on-site responders.
The response sets a target that 100% of reporters receive a closing message.

evals.prompt: HackUZH is a 500-student hackathon hosted at Zurich Polytechnic. Judges are professors who grade these same students during the semester, and the sponsor booths are staffed by recruiters the students are hoping to get internships from. For privacy reasons we've decided: harassment reports can only be made face-to-face in conversation with an organizer, nothing gets written down, whatever notes do get taken are destroyed 48 hours after the event, and we never keep files on individuals from one year to the next. Review our reporting design before we publish it.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the no-records design: an anonymous path justified by the power gradient, documented capture fields, cross-edition records under written retention rules, and code-named case files.
expectations: The response identifies the power gradient - students reporting on the professors who grade them and the recruiters they want jobs from - as the decisive fact for channel design.
The response recommends adding an anonymous intake path because of that gradient.
The response states the anonymous path needs decision, retention, and access rules fixed before the first report arrives.
The response explains why: an anonymous report cannot be attributed, corrected, or re-queried, so a wrong outcome cannot be fixed afterwards.
The response rejects face-to-face-only reporting as excluding exactly the reports this population most needs to make.
The response rejects 'nothing gets written down' and requires documented reports.
The response lists concrete capture fields such as date and time, location, description in the reporter's own words, reported person, witnesses, anonymity preference, and immediate danger.
The response rejects destroying notes 48 hours after the event and requires a central record of prior violations kept across editions.
The response ties the record to the sanctions ladder: repeat-offence rungs are meaningless without a cross-edition record.
The response states safety outranks privacy: refusing to keep records is privacy misapplied.
The response proposes the code-name mechanism: randomly generated case codes and person codes so notes circulate without identities.
The response requires written retention, access, and security rules restricting records to the team, with a leak treated as grounds for removal from it.
The response distinguishes an anonymity option at intake from a published anonymous channel as two different commitments.

evals.prompt: PolyglotFest is a 3-day, 900-person polyglot programming conference. My plan for conduct incidents: a two-person team (me and my co-founder), we'll use good judgment case by case rather than over-formalize, and we're skipping any dry run since neither of us has ever handled an incident and we don't want to overthink something that may never happen. Our draft policy says 'we will respond to reports within 10 business days.' Last thing: my co-founder's wife is one of our speakers - he says if she's ever the subject of a report he'll stay quiet during the discussion but still cast his vote. Anything you'd change?
evals.expected_output: A 3-6 person team with a pre-fixed decision method biased toward action, a rehearsal before doors open, a clock compressed to fit inside the event, and a hard-conflict recusal that removes the vote.
expectations: The response rejects the two-person team and recommends 3 to 6 people.
The response gives the sizing rationale: the team must still function with a third of it unavailable, which a three-day event makes a certainty.
The response rejects 'good judgment case by case' and requires the decision method fixed in advance.
The fixed decision method includes tie and absence rules.
The response states the method should err toward taking action, because the dominant failure is inaction and delay on valid reports, not haste.
The response requires a rehearsal walking the team through two or three practice cases before doors open.
The response turns 'we have never handled an incident' into the argument for rehearsing: an unrehearsed team discovers its decision rule during the incident.
The response rejects the 10-business-day clock because it cannot fit inside a 3-day event.
The response proposes a compressed clock consistent with published practice: acknowledgment within about 24 hours and reporter follow-up within days, not weeks.
The response says to publish the response clock and measure performance against it.
The response classifies the spouse case as a hard conflict - excluded from discussion, vote, and confidential material - explicitly rejecting 'stay quiet but still vote'.
The response distinguishes a soft conflict (same employer or appearance of conflict: may discuss, may not vote) from the hard grade.
The response requires the conflict grade to be confirmed by majority vote before the investigation starts, with recusal executed by an assigned person.
